When Sayyid Haydar Amuli states that a true Sufi is also a Shia, he is speaking from a profound understanding of shared spiritual heritage rather than demanding a formal change of allegiance. His assertion is rooted in the conviction that the deepest mystical insights of Sufism flow from the teachings of the Imams of the Ahl al-Bayt, whom he saw as the guides for the Sufi community just as they are for the Shia. For Amuli, the core of both paths is the same; he sought to show the compatibility and complementary nature of Twelver Shiism and Sufism.

The basis of this claim is **spiritual lineage**, not formal allegiance. Most Sufi orders trace their spiritual chain (سلسلة) back to the Prophet Muhammad through Maulana Ali. Maulana Ali is considered the fountainhead of the esoteric wisdom upon which Sufism is built. Amuli's point is that if a Sufi traces their spiritual roots back to their source, they will inevitably arrive at the Imams, who are the Prophet's family and the inheritors of his inner knowledge. In this view, to be a true Sufi is to recognize and embrace this foundational connection to the Imams.

A Sunni Sufi would likely accept the premise of this spiritual connection without difficulty. The veneration for Maulana Ali and the Ahl al-Bayt is a cornerstone of most Sufi traditions. They see Maulana Ali as a master of spiritual knowledge and a primary link in their lineage back to the Prophet. However, a Sunni Sufi would distinguish this spiritual reverence from the formal, doctrinal allegiance to the Imamate as understood in Shiism. They would honor the Imams as great saints and teachers but would not accept the Shia belief in their divine appointment as infallible political and religious successors to the Prophet.

Therefore, Amuli's statement is less a call for conversion and more an invitation to recognize a shared essence. He believed that a Sufi who truly understands the origins of their path would naturally be a Shia in spirit, because they would be drawing from the same wellspring of esoteric knowledge preserved and transmitted by the Imams. A Sunni Sufi could agree with the spiritual sentiment while maintaining their own distinct theological framework regarding the leadership of the Muslim community.

notes.body:
Picture the night sky wheeling overhead. Every star seems to drift, yet one point holds perfectly still — the pole star — and the whole turning heaven pivots around it. That fixed point is what the mystics mean by a Pole (قطب): **the living human being around whom the spiritual life of an entire age silently turns.**

The word is drawn straight from that image. A قطب is the pin an axle spins on, the pivot at the heart of a mill — the one motionless centre that makes all the movement around it possible. Applied to a person, it names the one whose heart is so fixed on Allah that others find their bearing through him, very often without ever knowing his name.

In the Sufi understanding this is a single hidden office, held by *one* person in each age — the summit of a whole company of saints ranked beneath him. When he passes another takes his place, so the line of guidance is never once broken.

The tradition then says the Imams of the Ahl al-Bayt were the *first* Poles (أقطاب) after the Prophet — in two senses at once:

- First in time — the earliest links in the chain, receiving the Prophet's spiritual blessing directly and handing it onward.
- First in rank — the very source from which every later Pole draws, the head of all the chains of masters.

An Imam holds this station not as a title he is granted but as a **function he embodies**. He is the friend and saint of Allah (ولی اللہ), the Pole of his own age, the one who unlocks the inner meaning of remembrance and himself initiates disciples into its practice. Every later master of the path traces his lineage back, hand to hand, until it comes to rest on Maulana Ali — the pivot on which the whole turning wheel of Islamic spirituality still quietly rests.
notes.anchor: These Imams were the first poles (aqtab, sing. qutb) of the spiritual…
notes.quote: These Imams were the first poles (aqtab, sing. qutb) of the spiritual tradition
etymology: قطب (Pole): from the root ق-ط-ب, the pivot-pin a millstone or an axle turns upon, and also the name of the pole star. The derived word keeps that sense of a single fixed centre around which everything else revolves — so a spiritual قطب is the still human axis of his whole age.

ولی (friend, saint): from the root و-ل-ي, meaning nearness — to stand beside something with no gap between. From it flow the senses of friend, protector and guardian. A ولی اللہ is one drawn so close to Allah that no distance remains, and through that nearness he guards and guides others.

أقطاب (Poles): the plural of قطب, sharing the same root ق-ط-ب. Where the singular names one pivot, the plural gathers the whole succession of them across the ages — each in turn the fixed centre of his own time, the Imams standing first among them.

notes.body:
Notice first that the Imam's phrase leaves a hole in the middle of itself. The sages 'befriend that by which the ignorant are estranged' — but the *that* is never named. **The blank is deliberate**, an open space each of us fills with whatever a fearful heart most wants to run from.

Fill it, and several honest readings open up:

- death, which the heedless dread and the wise walk toward
- affliction and hardship (بَلَاء), fled by the comfortable, embraced by the tested
- being alone (خَلْوَة), a terror to the restless and a gift to the seeker
- the emptying of the self (فَنَاء), the one loss the ego will do anything to avoid

Each is something the heedless one (غَافِل) instinctively escapes, and something the sage learns to sit beside as a companion.

So why does the chapter settle on prayer? Because **prayer quietly contains every item on that list**. Pure concentration on the Absolute is a small death, since the self and its noise are set aside; it is an affliction, because holding the mind still is hard, unglamorous work; and it asks for a kind of aloneness with Allah that most people flee. Prayer is not one more candidate beside the others — it is the room where all of them are gathered.

There is a second reason, closer to the surface. The whole passage is moving toward the remembrance of God (ذِكْر), and it arrives at this phrase by way of Junayd's praise of Maulana Ali as master of 'principles and affliction'. **The context has already chosen prayer** before the sentence lands; concentration is simply where that current was always flowing. The same silence that estranges the ignorant is, for the friend of Allah, the sweetest conversation he knows.
notes.anchor: befriend that by which the ignorant are estranged
notes.quote: befriend that by which the ignorant are estranged
etymology: بَلَاء (affliction): from the root ب-ل-و, whose sense is to wear out, test, or try — the way a garment is worn thin by long use. What tries us also wears us down, so the one root yields both the ordeal itself and the testing it works upon the soul.

خَلْوَة (retreat): from the root خ-ل-و, to be empty, vacant, alone. A place is called خالٍ when nothing fills it; the retreat is emptiness made deliberate — clearing the room of everyone and everything so that only Allah is left in it.

فَنَاء (self-effacement): from the root ف-ن-ي, to pass away, perish, come to an end. The word names the ego's passing — not ruin for its own sake, but the vanishing of the small self so that the divine Reality alone remains standing.

notes.body:
The word the Quran chooses here, أكبر, is left deliberately open. In Arabic it can mean 'greater' — greater than one named thing — or 'greatest' — the highest of all. **The commentators have read it in both senses at once**, and neither reading cancels the other.

Read the first way, remembrance is greater than the prayer just mentioned. Prayer fences us off from what is base, yet remembrance is the very life inside it — the awareness that we stand before Allah. Take that awareness away and only the motions remain; keep it, and it goes on illumining the heart long after we have risen from the mat.

Read the second way, remembrance is simply the greatest of all acts. This is how Maulana Ali speaks of it, naming it the most excellent worship (أفضل العبادة), and how the Prophet ranked the constant invocation above giving gold and silver and above facing the enemy in battle.

There is a third, tender reading the early companions loved, and it turns the phrase around. أكبر may mean that **Allah's remembrance of us is greater than our remembrance of Him**. We call on Him with a few faltering words; He answers by holding us within His awareness, and His is the boundless side of the exchange. The Quran promises this reciprocity:

فَٱذْكُرُونِىٓ أَذْكُرْكُمْ
'Remember Me, and I will remember you.'
Al-Baqarah 2:152

So the honest answer is that the verse carries all three, and they fold into one truth:

- greater than prayer, because remembrance is prayer's soul;
- greatest of all works, because everything else is done to keep it alive;
- greatest of all because the small remembrance we offer draws down the greater one He gives.

When we sit and say His Name, we are not beginning something. We are answering a call that reached us first.
notes.anchor: the remembrance of God is greater
notes.quote: the remembrance of God is greater
etymology: أكبر (greater/greatest): from the root ك-ب-ر, to be great in size or in rank. It is the elative form, which in Arabic serves as both comparative ('greater than') and superlative ('greatest'), so one word carries both a comparison and an absolute height — the grammar itself keeps the verse open to every reading.

ذكر (remembrance): from the root ذ-ك-ر, to recall and to mention. The root binds inner memory to outer utterance in a single word, so remembrance of Allah is at once a stirring of the heart and a word on the tongue — the thing held within made present again.

عبادة (worship): from the root ع-ب-د, to serve as a devoted servant; the same root gives عبد, a servant. Worship is thus not a task performed but the posture of belonging to Allah — which is why remembrance, the servant's turning toward the Master, is named its finest form.

notes.body:
Know Allah through Allah.

The difference between the two little words is the difference between a window and an eye. When we say a seeing happens *by* the heart, we make the heart the one who does the looking — the owner of the sight, the source of the act. When we say it happens *through* the heart, the heart becomes the clear place the looking passes through, while the real seer stands behind it. The passage chooses the second word: the vision of Allah is **not our own seeing of Allah but Allah's seeing of Allah, worked through the heart rather than by it.**

Why can it not be the heart's own act? A finite thing cannot take in the Infinite; no eye and no mind can wrap itself around what has no limit. The outer, human layer of the heart (قلب) is relative and small, but its innermost secret (سرّ) belongs, in truth, to the divine. So what sees is not the human rind of the heart but that hidden core, which is already Allah's.

Here the divine saying does the work. When Allah says of the one who draws near through extra devotions, "I am his hearing by which he hears, his sight by which he sees," the person's own faculties are quietly taken over. The remembrance (ذِكْر) polishes the heart until this can happen — the same picture Rumi gives of a breast burnished into a mirror. **A mirror never makes the image it shows; it only grows clean enough to return it.** The sun is not the glass's achievement.

So the knot unties in Maulana Ali's own compressed phrase:

اعرفوا الله بالله
Know Allah through Allah.

That small preposition (بـ) carries the whole point, meaning both 'by' and 'through' at once. It is Allah who both sees and is seen; the polished heart is only the place where that single act comes to rest. Our part is the polishing — the seeing was never ours to author.
notes.anchor: effected through the individual's 'heart' rather than by it
notes.quote: effected through the individual's 'heart' rather than by it
etymology: قلب (heart): from the root ق-ل-ب, to turn over, overturn, invert. From it come تَقَلُّب (fluctuation) and انقلاب (a turning-about). The heart is named for its restless turning, which is exactly why it must be polished and steadied before it can hold a single, steady vision.

سرّ (secret): from the root س-ر-ر, tied to what is hidden and folded away, and to the marrow within a bone. The سرّ is the innermost, concealed core of a thing — here the heart's deepest layer, the part kept from sight, which the passage says belongs in truth to the divine.

ذِكْر (remembrance): from the root ذ-ك-ر, to mention, to recall, to bring to mind. It names both the inward holding-present of a thing and its being spoken aloud. Here it is the polishing act that clears the heart until the seeing can pass through it.

بـ (by, through): the Arabic prepositional particle in بالله. It is deliberately wide, carrying 'by means of,' 'through,' and 'with' together. That breadth lets the phrase hold both readings at once — Allah known through Allah, and that knowing itself worked by Allah.

notes.body:
When Maulana Ali says "Know God through God," the point is startling: Allah is not something we arrive at by piling up evidence. We do not reason our way to Him from the world, and we do not catch Him with the senses. **He is known only by His own light** — the way the sun is seen by its own shining, never by a candle we hold up to it.

By what means, then? The means is Allah Himself. The heart, once polished by remembrance (ذِكْر), becomes a mirror, and what looks out through that mirror is no longer merely the human self. The hadith qudsi says of the one Allah loves, "I am his hearing by which he hears, his sight by which he sees." **The true seeing of Allah is Allah's own seeing**, worked through the servant's heart rather than by it.

This is why reasoning and the senses fall short: **both stand outside their object**, holding it at arm's length — the eye across from what it sees, the mind across from what it weighs. But nothing stands across from Allah; He is nearer to us than our own life-vein.

نَحْنُ أَقْرَبُ إِلَيْهِ مِنْ حَبْلِ الْوَرِيدِ
"And We are nearer to him than his jugular vein."
Qaf 50:16

Only a knowing in which the knower himself is effaced can reach a Reality that leaves no distance to cross.

How does this differ from the inborn nature (فِطْرَة) the chapter speaks of elsewhere? That inborn knowing is planted in us at the primordial covenant, buried like a treasure and merely forgotten; remembrance re-awakens it, and it is still *our* knowledge, recovered and made present again. Knowing Allah through Allah is the further shore, where **the separative self dissolves entirely** and it is Allah who knows Allah. The inborn nature is the seed sleeping in the soil; this is the ripe fruit, where the little self that once said "I know" is no longer there to say it.
etymology: معرفة (recognition, gnosis): from the root ع-ر-ف, whose sense is to know a thing again, to recognize what one has already met. This is why knowledge of Allah is spoken of as re-cognition — not fresh information, but the re-knowing of what the soul already carried.

بِاللّٰه (through Allah): the small prefix بِ carries the sense of "by means of," the instrument by which something is done. Set before the divine Name, it makes Allah not the object reached but the very tool of reaching — He is known by Himself.

فِطْرَة (inborn nature): from the root ف-ط-ر, to split or cleave open, and so to bring forth and originate. It is the nature we were cleaved-open into at creation, the original mould — hence a knowing present in us before any learning.

ذِكْر (remembrance): from the root ذ-ك-ر, to call to mind and to mention aloud. The single root holds both an inward presence and an outward utterance, which is why remembrance is at once a state of the heart and a word on the tongue.

When we insist that Allah is absolutely nondelimited, we create a mental category called 'nondelimitation' and place Him inside it. This very act of categorizing creates a boundary. By saying He is *only* nondelimited, we are distinguishing Him from the concept of 'delimitation', and this act of distinguishing is itself a limit. If Allah's absolute freedom could not even embrace limitation, it wouldn't be absolute freedom; it would be constrained by its own limitlessness. The statement 'then He is not He' suggests that the God confined by our neat, logical definition is no longer the true, all-encompassing Reality.

Instead of confining Allah to a single concept, we are meant to hold two seemingly opposite ideas together in our hearts. The first idea is transcendence (تَنْزِيه), which affirms that Allah is absolutely beyond and incomparable to anything in creation; this is His nondelimited aspect. The second idea is similarity (تَشْبِيه), which affirms that Allah is also immanent and manifest within creation, revealing His attributes through the world He has made. These are the "delimitations" He freely takes on.

The goal is to cultivate a spiritual vision that sees with two eyes, embracing both truths at once. We are to recognize Allah as simultaneously "other than every thing" and "with every thing." This is the profound work of the spiritual intellect (عَقْل), which must bind these two realities together to approach a more complete vision of the one Reality (ٱلْحَقّ).

***

تَنْزِيه (transcendence): From the root ن-ز-ه, meaning to be pure, clean, or far removed. In this context, it signifies declaring Allah's absolute purity from and distance from any comparison with created things. His reality is so far beyond our own that we cannot truly compare it to anything we know.

تَشْبِيه (similarity): From the root ش-ب-ه, meaning to resemble or be like something. This term points to the understanding that creation reflects the attributes of its Creator. We can see reflections of His knowledge, power, and beauty in the world, which makes Him, in a way, similar to it.

عَقْل (intellect): From the root ع-ق-ل, which means to bind, tie, or restrain. The intellect is the faculty that 'binds' ideas together to form a coherent understanding. In this spiritual context, its highest function is to bind the apparent opposites of transcendence and similarity into a unified perception of reality.
